themes: Plasma p-tau217 as a predictive biomarker
one_line: Plasma %p-tau217 clock models can estimate the time until Alzheimer's disease symptom onset in cognitively unimpaired individuals with a 3-4 year margin of error.
summary: This study developed biological clock models using longitudinal plasma %p-tau217 measurements from the Knight ADRC and ADNI cohorts to estimate the age of Alzheimer's disease (AD) symptom onset in cognitively unimpaired individuals. The authors identified an interval of consistent biomarker change and applied Temporal Integration of Rate Accumulation (TIRA) and Sampled Iterative Local Approximation (SILA) methodologies to align individualized trajectories. They found a moderate-to-strong association between the estimated age at %p-tau217 positivity and the age at AD symptom onset, showing a median absolute error of 3.0 to 3.7 years. Notably, the data revealed that older individuals developed AD symptoms much sooner after reaching biomarker positivity than younger individuals. The clock modeling approach also generalized successfully to other p-tau217 and p-tau217/Aβ42 immunoassays. While the 3-to-4-year error margin limits definitive individual prognostic utility, the models could significantly improve clinical trial efficiency by enriching cohorts with individuals highly likely to develop symptoms within the trial's timeframe.

key_claims.claim: Plasma %p-tau217 clock models can estimate the age of AD symptom onset in cognitively unimpaired individuals.
key_claims.evidence: The estimated age at plasma %p-tau217 positivity was associated with the age at onset of AD symptoms (adjusted R2 of 0.337−0.612) with a median absolute error of 3.0−3.7 years.
key_claims.location: Abstract / Results (Predicting the age of AD symptom onset)

key_claims.claim: The time interval from %p-tau217 biomarker positivity to the onset of AD symptoms is markedly shorter in older individuals.
key_claims.evidence: Participants who became plasma %p-tau217 positive at age 60 had a median time until symptom onset of 20.5 years, whereas participants who became positive at age 80 had a median time until symptom onset of only 11.4 years.
key_claims.location: Results (Modeling the probability of developing symptomatic AD)

key_claims.claim: The clock modeling approach generalizes across different commercially available plasma p-tau217 and p-tau217/Aβ42 assays.
key_claims.evidence: Similar predictive clock models were successfully constructed with data from one Fujirebio Lumipulse p-tau217/Aβ42 immunoassay and four other plasma p-tau217 immunoassays (C2N, Janssen, ALZpath, Fujirebio).

methods.population: Community-dwelling older adults (cognitively unimpaired and impaired) from the Knight ADRC (n=258) and ADNI (n=345) cohorts.
methods.duration: Median follow-up interval of 6.5 years (Knight ADRC) and 4.5 years (ADNI)

funding_and_conflicts: Funded by the FNIH Biomarkers Consortium, NIA, ADNI, DOD, and multiple pharmaceutical/diagnostic companies (AbbVie, Alzheimer’s Association, Biogen, Janssen, Takeda). Significant conflicts of interest exist: numerous authors are employees, stock owners, patent inventors, or advisory board members for companies deeply involved in Alzheimer's diagnostics and therapeutics (including C2N Diagnostics, Eli Lilly, Biogen, Takeda, Johnson & Johnson, and AbbVie).
limitations: Clock models can only be utilized for %p-tau217 values strictly within the interval of consistent change (1.06% to 10.45%), limiting applicability for very high or low values.
The median absolute error of 3-4 years limits the model's utility for individual clinical decision-making.
The study cohorts were largely non-Hispanic White, potentially limiting generalizability across diverse populations.
Participant dropout or death was not explicitly modeled, which may introduce survival bias by underestimating decline among the most vulnerable individuals.
red_flags: Heavy financial and patent involvement from diagnostic companies (e.g., C2N Diagnostics) and pharmaceutical companies whose products are being evaluated.
Post-hoc derivation of the 'interval of consistent change' (variance below the 90th percentile) to restrict data could introduce overfitting or limit real-world predictive validity.
